concepts.def: The Nazi 'coordination' of German society from 1933, bringing political parties, trade unions, media and culture under party control.
Nazi youth movements indoctrinating boys for military service and girls (League of German Maidens) for motherhood; membership was made effectively compulsory by 1939.
Policy pushed women towards 'Kinder, Küche, Kirche' — children, kitchen, church — with marriage loans and the Mother's Cross rewarding large families.
Goebbels' Ministry of Propaganda controlled press, film and radio, using rallies, cheap radio sets and spectacles like the 1936 Berlin Olympics to glorify the regime.
The secret state police and SS enforced conformity through surveillance, informers, arbitrary arrest and the concentration camp system.
Escalating persecution from boycotts in 1933 through the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 and Kristallnacht in 1938 to the wartime Holocaust.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Life in Nazi Germany 1933-45 — a core area of GCSE History.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Life in Nazi Germany 1933-45 brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Life in Nazi Germany 1933-45.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What did the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 do?
options: Stripped German Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews
Banned the Nazi Party from holding rallies
Introduced rationing across Germany
Made church attendance compulsory

mcqs.q: Who was the Nazi Minister of Propaganda?
options: Joseph Goebbels
Heinrich Himmler
Hermann Göring
Rudolf Hess

mcqs.q: What did the slogan 'Kinder, Küche, Kirche' expect of German women?
options: To devote themselves to children, the home and church rather than careers
To serve in the armed forces
To run Nazi propaganda offices
To work in heavy industry instead of having families

mcqs.q: What happened on Kristallnacht in November 1938?
options: Coordinated attacks destroyed synagogues and Jewish businesses, and around 30,000 Jewish men were sent to camps
The Berlin Olympics opened
Hitler was appointed Chancellor
The German army occupied the Rhineland

mcqs.q: Did all young Germans enthusiastically support the Hitler Youth?
options: Every young German was an enthusiastic Nazi because of indoctrination.
The Hitler Youth was banned by the Nazis themselves in 1939.
Persecution of Jews only ever happened outside Germany's borders.
Many enjoyed the camps and sport, but by the war years groups such as the Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth openly rejected Nazi youth culture.

mcqs.q: Was the Gestapo watching everyone in Nazi Germany?
options: The Gestapo was the German army's tank division.
Persecution of Jews only ever happened outside Germany's borders.
The Gestapo was actually a fairly small organisation that relied heavily on denunciations volunteered by ordinary citizens.
The Gestapo had agents permanently stationed on every street corner.

mcqs.q: Did Nazi persecution of the Jews begin with death camps in 1933?
options: Persecution escalated step by step — the 1933 boycott, the 1935 Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht in 1938, then ghettos and mass murder during the war.
Persecution of Jews only ever happened outside Germany's borders.
The Gestapo was the German army's tank division.
Extermination camps were operating from the moment Hitler took power.
